idiom_name: Symbol.toPrimitive coercion hooks plus prototype/Object.assign mixins (methods only)
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no operator overloading: the only hooks the language consults are Symbol.toPrimitive (and the valueOf/toString pair it supersedes) for the coercions that +, <, == and template literals perform, so a class can influence the primitive an expression produces but can never return a new instance of itself from a + b. Family-wide behaviour is delivered as methods through prototype chains or mixins (Object.assign copies enumerable own properties, Object.defineProperty/Object.getOwnPropertySymbols copy the rest), which is why 'mixin operators' has no counterpart. For arithmetic-like types (money, decimals, vectors) the honest shape is explicit methods - add, mul, cmp - or a library that documents the method contract, not operator syntax.
alternative: Explicit named methods (Money.plus, Money.compareTo, Version.isLessThan) with shared implementations mixed into prototypes, plus Symbol.toPrimitive/valueOf only for the coercions the language performs itself; operator syntax for user types does not exist in JavaScript.
pitfalls: Symbol.toPrimitive must return a primitive or the runtime throws a TypeError, so the coercion route can never synthesise a new instance of your class.
Coercion failures are silent: without a valueOf/Symbol.toPrimitive, a + b concatenates strings ('[object Object]') and < compares garbage instead of raising.

Object.assign copies only enumerable own properties (so non-enumerable or symbol-keyed methods need Object.defineProperty/Object.getOwnPropertySymbols), and copied methods lose access to the source class's #private fields.
